record.original_question: Does there exist a polynomial f(x,y) with rational coefficients such that the induced map f: Q x Q -> Q is a bijection, meaning that for every rational number q there is exactly one pair of rational numbers (x,y) with f(x,y)=q?

evidence.quote: Is there any polynomial f(x,y)\in{\mathbb Q}[x,y]{} such that f\colon\mathbb{Q}\times\mathbb{Q} \rightarrow\mathbb{Q} is a bijection?

artifact.self_contained_problem: Does there exist a polynomial $f(x,y) \in \mathbb{Q}[x,y]$ such that the induced map $f \colon \mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Q}$, $(x,y) \mapsto f(x,y)$, is a bijection? That is, is there a two-variable polynomial with rational coefficients such that for every rational number $q$ there exists exactly one pair $(x,y) \in \mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q}$ with $f(x,y) = q$?
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is widely regarded as open. Conditional results exist: Poonen showed (assuming the Bombieri–Lang conjecture together with another conjecture) the existence of polynomial injections $\mathbb{Q}\times\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}$, and Bresciani has obtained conditional results ruling out such bijections over number fields under Bombieri–Lang. No unconditional resolution is known.

status_evidence.title: Ruling out polynomial bijections over the rationals via Bombieri-Lang?
status_evidence.snippet: Whether there exist any polynomials of two variables with rational coefficients such that the map P: Q x Q -> Q is a bijection is a famous open question.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is a famous open question; conditional results under Bombieri-Lang exist.

status_evidence.title: A sort of Polymath on a famous MathOverflow problem
status_evidence.snippet: The answer is almost surely 'no', but it is remarkable how hard this problem resists any attempt at rigorous proof.
